RELIGIOUS ACCOMMODATION IN EMPLOYMENT (FEHA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) requirement that an employer reasonably accommodate an employee's or applicant's religious belief or observance, Government Code section 12940(l), as it relates to Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee. It states facts about what the statute requires, the statutory definitions of "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice," the statute's own definition of "undue hardship," and the statute's specific rule that segregating an employee is not a reasonable accommodation. Religious accommodation is a category of FEHA coverage distinct from the physical- and mental-disability accommodation requirement in Government Code section 12940(m) and from the genetic-information provisions of the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act; this document does not restate those other bodies of law and is not itself a request for accommodation, a determination that any accommodation is or is not required, or an interactive-process record. It does not tell Acme, Inc. or Jordan Lee whether any specific request, practice, or belief qualifies for accommodation under the statute, whether providing or denying any specific accommodation would create undue hardship, or what to do about any specific situation.

FAILURE TO REASONABLY ACCOMMODATE RELIGIOUS BELIEF OR OBSERVANCE IS AN UNLAWFUL EMPLOYMENT PRACTICE
California's Fair Employment and Housing Act makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer or other entity covered by the Act to refuse to hire or employ a person, to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment, to bar or discharge a person from employment or a training program, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of a conflict between the person's religious belief or observance and an employment requirement. This prohibition applies unless the employer or other covered entity demonstrates that it has explored any available reasonable alternative means of accommodating the religious belief or observance -- including the possibility of excusing the person from the conflicting duties or permitting those duties to be performed at another time or by another person -- but is unable to reasonably accommodate the religious belief or observance without undue hardship on the conduct of its business. By its own terms, the statute applies to apprenticeship training programs, unpaid internships, and other unpaid workplace experience programs, not only to paid employment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(l) (1) For an employer or other entity covered by this part to refuse to hire or employ a person or to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment or to bar or to discharge a person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of a conflict between the person’s religious belief or observance and any employment requirement, unless the employer or other entity covered by this part demonstrates that it has explored any available reasonable alternative means of accommodating the religious belief or observance, including the possibilities of excusing the person from those duties that conflict with the person’s religious belief or observance or permitting those duties to be performed at another time or by another person, but is unable to reasonably accommodate the religious belief or observance without undue hardship, as defined in subdivision (u) of Section 12926, on the conduct of the business of the employer or other entity covered by this part."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(1), California Fair Employment and Housing Act, unlawful employment practices -- failure to reasonably accommodate religious belief or observance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory paragraph, Government Code section 12940(l)(1), quoted in full below; it is not corroborated by a second, independent statutory source. The statute cross-references its own definition of "undue hardship" (Government Code section 12926(u)) and its own definitions of "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice" (Government Code section 12926(q)); those definitions are quoted and discussed in separate clauses below rather than repeated here. This clause states only that the described conduct is an unlawful employment practice under the statute; it does not determine whether any specific employer's treatment of any specific individual was because of a religious belief or observance, and it does not determine whether any specific accommodation was reasonably available or would have caused undue hardship.

"RELIGIOUS DRESS PRACTICE" AND "RELIGIOUS GROOMING PRACTICE" ARE SPECIFICALLY DEFINED
The FEHA religious-accommodation requirement expressly states that "religious belief or observance," as used in the accommodation section, includes but is not limited to observance of a Sabbath or other religious holy day or days, reasonable time necessary for travel before and after a religious observance, and religious dress practice and religious grooming practice as those terms are described in a separate FEHA definitions section, Government Code section 12926(q). That definitions section states that "religious creed," "religion," "religious observance," "religious belief," and "creed" include all aspects of religious belief, observance, and practice, including religious dress and grooming practices, and it defines "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice" as terms to be construed broadly. "Religious dress practice" is defined to include the wearing or carrying of religious clothing, head or face coverings, jewelry, artifacts, and any other item that is part of an individual observing a religious creed. "Religious grooming practice" is defined to include all forms of head, facial, and body hair that are part of an individual observing a religious creed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Religious belief or observance, as used in this section, includes, but is not limited to, observance of a Sabbath or other religious holy day or days, reasonable time necessary for travel prior and subsequent to a religious observance, and religious dress practice and religious grooming practice as described in subdivision (q) of Section 12926. This subdivision shall also apply to an apprenticeship training program, an unpaid internship, and any other program to provide unpaid experience for a person in the workplace or industry."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(1), FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- religious belief or observance includes religious dress and grooming practice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940)
  "“Religious creed,” “religion,” “religious observance,” “religious belief,” and “creed” include all aspects of religious belief, observance, and practice, including religious dress and grooming practices. “Religious dress practice” shall be construed broadly to include the wearing or carrying of religious clothing, head or face coverings, jewelry, artifacts, and any other item that is part of an individual observing a religious creed. “Religious grooming practice” shall be construed broadly to include all forms of head, facial, and body hair that are part of an individual observing a religious creed."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(q), FEHA definitions -- "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926)
  Known gap: This clause combines two citations that are not independent corroboration of each other: Government Code section 12940(l)(1) is the accommodation requirement itself, and it establishes that religious dress and grooming practices are covered only by cross-referencing Government Code section 12926(q), a separate definitions section within the same FEHA definitions statute that supplies the actual defined terms. The 12940(l)(1) language quoted here is the same paragraph already quoted in the preceding clause on the core prohibition, so this clause is also not independent of that one. This clause states the statutory definitions only; it does not determine whether any specific item of clothing, head or face covering, jewelry, artifact, or form of hair in any specific case is part of an individual observing a religious creed within the meaning of the statute.

FEHA'S OWN "UNDUE HARDSHIP" STANDARD
The religious-accommodation requirement does not define "undue hardship" in its own text; it cross-refers to a general definition set out elsewhere in FEHA, Government Code section 12926(u), that applies to undue-hardship determinations throughout the Act, not only to religious accommodation. That definition states that "undue hardship" means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, considered in light of five listed factors: the nature and cost of the accommodation needed; the overall financial resources of the facility or facilities involved and the effect of the accommodation on the facility's expenses, resources, or operations; the overall financial resources of the covered entity, including its overall size and the number, type, and location of its facilities; the type of operations of the entity, including the composition, structure, and functions of its workforce; and the geographic separateness or administrative or fiscal relationship of the facility or facilities. This is a multi-factor balancing test defined directly in the statute's text, not left to case law to define from scratch.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Undue hardship” means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, when considered in light of the following factors: (1) The nature and cost of the accommodation needed. (2) The overall financial resources of the facilities involved in the provision of the reasonable accommodations, the number of persons employed at the facility, and the effect on expenses and resources or the impact otherwise of these accommodations upon the operation of the facility. (3) The overall financial resources of the covered entity, the overall size of the business of a covered entity with respect to the number of employees, and the number, type, and location of its facilities. (4) The type of operations, including the composition, structure, and functions of the workforce of the entity. (5) The geographic separateness or administrative or fiscal relationship of the facility or facilities."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(u), FEHA definitions -- "undue hardship" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, Government Code section 12926(u), which is a different, independently numbered section of the Government Code from section 12940 (the accommodation requirement itself); it is used here because section 12940(l)(1) cross-refers to it by name, and that cross-reference is quoted in the core-prohibition clause above rather than repeated here. Federal Title VII also imposes a duty to accommodate religious practice, and its "undue hardship" standard was addressed by the U.S. Supreme Court in Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023); this document does not independently verify the text of the federal statute or the Groff opinion, does not restate the federal standard, and does not state whether the state and federal standards would produce the same result in any given case -- a reader should not assume FEHA's defined standard is identical to the federal one. This clause states the statutory factors only; it does not determine whether any specific accommodation would require significant difficulty or expense in any specific case.

SEGREGATING AN EMPLOYEE IS NOT A REASONABLE ACCOMMODATION OF RELIGIOUS DRESS OR GROOMING
The statute states directly that an accommodation of an individual's religious dress practice or religious grooming practice is not reasonable if the accommodation requires segregation of the individual from other employees or from the public. This is a specific rule stated in the text of the statute itself, not a general inference from the reasonable-accommodation requirement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(2) An accommodation of an individual’s religious dress practice or religious grooming practice is not reasonable if the accommodation requires segregation of the individual from other employees or the public."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(2), FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- segregation is not a reasonable accommodation of religious dress or grooming practice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(2), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the core prohibition quoted above; it is not an independent statutory source from that clause, though it states a distinct, specific rule within that subdivision. This clause states the statutory rule only; it does not describe what would or would not constitute "segregation" in any specific workplace arrangement, and it does not address accommodations of religious belief or observance generally (as opposed to religious dress or grooming practice specifically), which the statute's text ties this particular rule to.

AN ACCOMMODATION IS NOT REQUIRED IF IT WOULD ITSELF VIOLATE THE LAW
The statute states that an accommodation is not required under the religious-accommodation subdivision if it would result in a violation of the Fair Employment and Housing Act itself or of any other law prohibiting discrimination or protecting civil rights, including the Unruh Civil Rights Act's prohibition on business-establishment discrimination (Civil Code section 51(b)) and the state's general prohibition on discrimination in state-funded and state-conducted programs and activities (Government Code section 11135).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(3) An accommodation is not required under this subdivision if it would result in a violation of this part or any other law prohibiting discrimination or protecting civil rights, including subdivision (b) of Section 51 of the Civil Code and Section 11135 of this code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(3), FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- accommodation not required if it would violate antidiscrimination law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(3), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the core prohibition and segregation clauses above; it is not an independent statutory source from those clauses. This clause identifies the two other statutes the text cross-references by name; it does not restate or quote the text of Civil Code section 51(b) or Government Code section 11135 themselves, and it does not determine whether any specific accommodation would in fact violate either of those laws or any other antidiscrimination law in any specific case.

REQUESTING A RELIGIOUS ACCOMMODATION IS A PROTECTED ACT, REGARDLESS OF OUTCOME
The statute separately makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer or other covered entity to retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting a religious accommodation, regardless of whether the request was granted. The statute states this protection is in addition to the general retaliation protections that apply to opposing practices forbidden under FEHA or filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in any proceeding under the Act.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(4) For an employer or other entity covered by this part to, in addition to the employee protections provided pursuant to subdivision (h), retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting accommodation under this subdivision, regardless of whether the request was granted."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(4), FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- retaliation for requesting religious accommodation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12940)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(4), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the clauses above; it is not an independent statutory source from those clauses. This clause does not restate or quote the general retaliation-protection subdivision, section 12940(h), that this paragraph cross-references; it states only that the religious-accommodation retaliation protection applies regardless of whether the underlying request was granted, and it does not determine whether any specific adverse treatment of any specific individual was retaliation for requesting an accommodation.

WHICH EMPLOYERS ARE COVERED: THE FIVE-EMPLOYEE THRESHOLD
FEHA's employment provisions, including the religious-accommodation requirement, apply to an "employer" as FEHA's own definitions section defines that term. That definition states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, subject to stated exceptions. The definition further states that "employer" does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows: “Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d), FEHA definitions -- "employer," five-or-more-employees threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12926)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12926(d), which is a different, independently numbered section of the Government Code from section 12940 (the accommodation requirement itself), but it is a different subdivision of the same section 12926 already relied on in the dress/grooming-definitions and undue-hardship clauses above, so it is not independent corroboration of those clauses' points -- all three (subdivisions (d), (q), and (u) of section 12926) are drawn from the same definitions statute. The religious-accommodation subdivision, section 12940(l), applies by its own terms to "an employer or other entity covered by this part," a broader phrase than "employer" alone; this clause addresses only the numerical threshold for "employer" and does not verify what threshold, if any, applies to the other categories of covered entity (such as labor organizations or employment agencies) that the broader phrase may also reach. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not determine whether any specific entity regularly employs five or more persons in any given period, and it does not address the religious-association-or-nonprofit exclusion's scope beyond quoting it.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate that you have received and reviewed this information sheet.

Applicant / Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
